PhysLDM: Latent Diffusion for
High-Fidelity Deformable Simulation

Yu Zhang   Xudong Xu   Xingang Pan S-Lab, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, Shanghai, China {yuzhang,xingang.pan}@ntu.edu.sg   xudongxu9710@gmail.com
Abstract

Neural simulation of high-fidelity deformable bodies is a foundational challenge in computer graphics and physical AI. Long-horizon prediction for high-resolution 3D volumetric meshes is difficult: autoregressive methods are susceptible to error accumulation, while direct multi-frame prediction at native resolution is computationally prohibitive. This motivates a compact spatiotemporal latent representation, which remains largely unexplored for mesh-based volumetric physics. Meanwhile, it remains unclear whether deterministic regression or generative diffusion is the more appropriate predictive paradigm. To address these coupled challenges, we introduce PhysLDM, a unified latent-diffusion paradigm for one-shot volumetric deformable simulation. Its core is a holistic spatiotemporal VAE (ST-VAE) that avoids the “staircase” artifacts of standard temporal compression (as in common video VAEs) and disentangles rigid motion from local deformation, achieving ∼\sim2.48 mm reconstruction precision on meter-scale scenes at up to 78×\times token compression. Based on this reliable latent space, we systematically compare regression and diffusion paradigms. Our experiments uncover a key modeling insight: complex deformable dynamics are often chaotic, and in this regime deterministic regression tends to produce damped, non-physical averages, whereas diffusion better models their distribution. Accordingly, we employ a latent diffusion model that effectively learns from the chaotic data to generate physically plausible trajectories. Trained purely kinematically on an Objaverse-scale simulation dataset, a single PhysLDM generalizes zero-shot to unseen OOD object datasets (GSO and Toys4K). Its differentiability further enables efficient solution of inverse problems and higher-order design optimization. To our knowledge, PhysLDM is the first high-fidelity spatiotemporal autoencoder and latent-diffusion paradigm for volumetric deformable dynamics, offering a scalable and robust approach to neural simulation. Project Page: https://yucrazing.github.io/physldm/

1 Introduction

Simulating the dynamics of deformable solids is essential to fields involving physical interaction, including computer graphics, engineering, and robotics. Furthermore, learning these complex dynamics as predictive physical world models is also considered essential for physical AI. However, fulfilling this vision with traditional simulators remains a fundamental bottleneck: classical high-precision solvers are accurate but slow, and their gradients are hard to obtain. Neural simulation is an emerging alternative: its goal is to learn these complex physical behaviors directly from data, offering fast, differentiable surrogates that bypass the computational bottlenecks of classical solvers (Sanchez-Gonzalez et al., 2020; Pfaff et al., 2021). Nevertheless, high-fidelity deformable simulation demands a high-resolution geometric representation, typically a volumetric mesh with thousands to tens of thousands of vertices. Efficiently and accurately predicting the long-horizon trajectories of such large-scale systems poses significant challenges for conventional neural architectures.

Achieving this, however, presents several tightly coupled challenges. First, high-fidelity 3D volumetric meshes contain large, object-dependent numbers of vertices, resulting in extremely high-dimensional system states. Existing autoregressive (AR) approaches predict the dynamics frame by frame, without jointly modeling the full temporal horizon, and are therefore susceptible to compounding errors and trajectory drift over long rollouts. One-shot prediction of the entire trajectory provides global temporal context, but operating directly at native resolution is computationally prohibitive. Consequently, compressing these complex dynamics into a spatiotemporal latent space becomes necessary, yet largely unexplored for mesh-based volumetric physics. This introduces the first challenge: a representational bottleneck. In our explorations, we find that standard compression methods (e.g., with uniform temporal strides and local temporal upsamplers, as in standard video-VAE designs (Yu et al., 2023)) lose high-frequency temporal information and make reconstructed shapes jump unnaturally, producing a “staircase” artifact that we analyze in Sec. 4 (Staircase analysis). Furthermore, directly compressing raw world coordinates forces models to entangle large-scale rigid motion with millimeter-scale local deformations, severely degrading precision.

The second challenge is the optimal predictive paradigm: it remains an open question whether deterministic regression or generative diffusion is better suited for complex physical simulation, and a systematic comparison in the context of 3D volumetric physics is currently absent. Our systematic experiments reveal a critical insight: microscopic non-determinism can be strongly amplified by the inherently chaotic nature of complex deformable dynamics. For instance, state-of-the-art GPU-based physical solvers (Huang et al., 2024a; Huang et al., 2025) exhibit only slight microscopic non-determinism, yet chaos can amplify this small difference into vastly different final trajectories (Sec. 4, Chaos analysis). In this chaotic regime, nearly identical initial conditions can correspond to multiple macroscopically different yet physically plausible futures. Deterministic regression tends to average over these modes, producing damped trajectories that may match none of them, whereas generative diffusion can represent and sample from the multi-modal distribution of plausible outcomes.

To overcome these tightly coupled representational and predictive limitations, we propose PhysLDM, a latent-diffusion paradigm for one-shot volumetric deformable simulation. The foundation of PhysLDM is a novel holistic spatiotemporal variational autoencoder (ST-VAE) specifically designed for mesh-based volumetric physics. By employing a holistic temporal compression strategy and explicitly decoupling rigid body motion from local deformation, our ST-VAE eliminates “staircase” artifacts and preserves fine geometric details. This design achieves a ∼\sim2.48 mm average geometric reconstruction precision for meter-scale scenes at up to a 78×78\times token compression. By employing a Latent Diffusion Model (LDM) (Rombach et al., 2022), PhysLDM models the distribution of physically plausible future trajectories, whereas deterministic regression produces damped averages in our experiments.

A prominent feature of our paradigm is its constitutive-model-agnostic nature. Supervised purely kinematically on an Objaverse-scale dataset, a single PhysLDM demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization capabilities to unseen, out-of-distribution (OOD) datasets. We further demonstrate the utility of PhysLDM as a differentiable simulator for inverse problems and design optimization. To our knowledge, PhysLDM yields the first high-fidelity spatiotemporal autoencoder and latent-diffusion paradigm for volumetric deformable dynamics, offering a scalable and robust approach to neural simulation.

In summary, our main contributions include:

  • •

    A high-fidelity ST-VAE for 3D volumetric deformable dynamics. We propose a novel holistic temporal compression scheme for volumetric mesh deformable dynamics, which removes the “staircase” artifacts that persist under standard temporal compression. By explicitly decoupling rigid motion and deformation, we achieve ∼\sim2.48mm average geometric reconstruction precision for meter-scale scenes with up to 78×\times token compression.

  • •

    A systematic comparison of deterministic regression and generative diffusion paradigms in physical simulation. We reveal that the inherently chaotic nature of complex deformable dynamics can amplify the non-determinism that GPU solvers exhibit under identical initial conditions, and show that in this chaotic regime diffusion is better suited than deterministic regression, whose outputs collapse toward damped averages.

  • •

    A constitutive-model-agnostic latent diffusion paradigm with strong zero-shot generalization. We present a latent-diffusion paradigm and train a single model, PhysLDM, on Objaverse-scale simulations (Deitke et al., 2023) supervised purely kinematically. Our model transfers zero-shot to unseen OOD object datasets (GSO (Downs et al., 2022), Toys4K (Stojanov et al., 2021)) with remarkable robustness.

  • •

    A differentiable simulator for inverse problems and design optimization. PhysLDM supports end-to-end and higher-order differentiation, enabling efficient material estimation and second-order design optimization tasks that are difficult or computationally prohibitive for existing differentiable simulators.

2 Related Work

Physics-based deformable simulation. Physics-based Lagrangian simulation has a rich history in computer graphics, evolving from early elastic models (Terzopoulos et al., 1987) to finite element methods (FEM) (Irving et al., 2004), contact handling (Bridson et al., 2002), and others (Müller et al., 2007; Bouaziz et al., 2014). Recently, barrier-based methods such as incremental potential contact (IPC) provide strict intersection-free guarantees, but incur high computational costs (Li et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2024a; Huang et al., 2025; Tang et al., 2026; Ando, 2024). Conversely, real-time solvers achieve interactive rates at the expense of physical fidelity, and they cannot learn the behavior of high-accuracy solvers (Chen et al., 2024; Giles et al., 2025). Differentiable simulators restore gradients, but either require tedious hand-derived formulations or need to backpropagate through every integration step (Huang et al., 2024b; The Newton Contributors, 2025). In contrast, PhysLDM serves as a fast, end-to-end differentiable neural surrogate learned directly from high-accuracy solvers.

Neural simulators for deformable dynamics. Neural simulators provide a fast, fully differentiable alternative to traditional solvers. The dominant paradigm of neural simulators is the AR rollout, which predicts the next state frame-by-frame. This paradigm has been adopted across diverse physical simulation fields (Sanchez-Gonzalez et al., 2020; Ummenhofer et al., 2020; Pfaff et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026). However, AR methods lack the global temporal context necessary for long-horizon consistency, potentially leading to temporal incoherence or trajectory drift. The concurrent work of Chen et al. (2026) performs one-shot multi-frame prediction, but is restricted to low-resolution surface meshes (training on about 356356 vertices per scene) from a limited set of templates (3535 different meshes). In contrast, PhysLDM introduces a latent-diffusion paradigm capable of predicting high-resolution volumetric trajectories in a single diffusion pass, demonstrating strong zero-shot generalization to diverse OOD scenes.

Spatiotemporal latent representations. High-fidelity volumetric simulation involves high-resolution meshes, making direct multi-frame prediction computationally prohibitive at native resolutions. However, spatiotemporal autoencoders remain largely unexplored for high-fidelity, volumetric-mesh deformable-body physical simulation. In fact, existing autoencoders for physical simulation typically compress only the spatial domain (Barbic and James, 2005; Fulton et al., 2019; Romero et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2023; Chang et al., 2023; Modi et al., 2024; Liao et al., 2026; Wiewel et al., 2019; Han et al., 2022), with concurrent neural simulators following a similar pattern (Zhang et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026; Geng et al., 2026). While spatiotemporal autoencoders have been successfully deployed in other domains, their architectures are tailored to their respective tasks, such as video generation (Yu et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025) and other fields (Petrovich et al., 2021; Cao et al., 2024). Unfortunately, these designs do not transfer directly to deformable physics. For example, transplanting the standard temporal compression of video VAEs produces severe staircase artifacts (as analyzed in Sec. 4, Staircase analysis). To our knowledge, our ST-VAE is the first spatiotemporal autoencoder designed specifically for high-fidelity deformable simulation.

Prediction paradigms: regression versus diffusion. For deformable-body physical simulation, deterministic regression and generative diffusion have never been systematically compared. In practice, most work in neural simulation uses regression (Sanchez-Gonzalez et al., 2020; Pfaff et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2026; Dou et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026). Meanwhile, diffusion (Ho et al., 2020) has instead been adopted where output distributions matter, such as image and video synthesis (Rombach et al., 2022; Ho et al., 2022) and human motion (Tevet et al., 2023). Although the concurrent work of Chen et al. (2026) claims that diffusion is superior to deterministic regression, motivated by the diversity of futures under unobserved initial conditions, it never compares one-shot regression with diffusion. By contrast, we systematically compare both paradigms and find that under the chaotic dynamics of complex deformable bodies diffusion is more suitable, and regression may collapse onto non-physical averages.

3 Methodology

3.1 Problem Formulation

We formulate the physical simulation of volumetric objects as a trajectory prediction task. Let a scene be represented as a tetrahedral mesh with rest vertices 𝐫∈ℝN×3\mathbf{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 3}. The initial state of the system is defined as 𝐬0=(𝐫,𝐑0,𝐜0,𝐯0,𝝎0,E)\mathbf{s}_{0}=(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{R}_{0},\mathbf{c}_{0},\mathbf{v}_{0},\boldsymbol{\omega}_{0},E), which encompasses the rest geometry, the frame-00 pose, linear velocity, and angular velocity, together with the Young’s modulus EE of the material. Our goal is to model the distribution p⁡(𝐗∣𝐬0)p(\mathbf{X}\mid\mathbf{s}_{0}) of future vertex trajectories 𝐗∈ℝT×N×3\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times N\times 3} over a horizon of TT frames. Rather than modeling the raw world coordinates directly, we factor each frame into a global rigid transform acting on a canonical deformation:

𝐱t=𝐑t​(𝐫+𝐝t)+𝐜t,\mathbf{x}_{t}=\mathbf{R}_{t}\,(\mathbf{r}+\mathbf{d}_{t})+\mathbf{c}_{t}, (1)

where 𝐑t∈SO⁡(3)\mathbf{R}_{t}\in\mathrm{SO}(3) and 𝐜t∈ℝ3\mathbf{c}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} denote the per-frame rigid rotation and centroid translation, and 𝐝t\mathbf{d}_{t} represents the residual canonical (rigid-free) deformation field. 𝐑t\mathbf{R}_{t} and 𝐜t\mathbf{c}_{t} are extracted from each ground-truth frame in closed form by a per-frame Procrustes (Kabsch) fit of the rest shape (Umeyama, 1991). This factoring separates the large-scale rigid motion from the small-scale deformation. The rigid transform (𝐑t,𝐜t)(\mathbf{R}_{t},\mathbf{c}_{t}) carries the global motion in six degrees of freedom per frame. The canonical deformation field 𝐝t\mathbf{d}_{t} then only has to capture the local deformation, which is independent of the object’s pose.

3.2 Architecture Overview

As shown in Figure 2, PhysLDM has three main modules: a Spatial VAE, an ST-VAE, and an LDM.

Spatial VAE. To efficiently process high-resolution volumetric meshes of varying vertex counts, we compress individual frames using a Spatial VAE. Following the representation of Zhang et al. (2026), a set of KK learnable query tokens cross-attends the canonical mesh vertices to extract a fixed-size set of KK latent tokens 𝐳t\mathbf{z}_{t}, which remains independent of the vertex count NN. The decoder mirrors the encoder: each rest vertex, embedded with its position, cross-attends the latent tokens and is decoded to its displacement. This module ensures that the latent representation is resolution-independent.

ST-VAE. The ST-VAE compresses the input TT-frame trajectory by a factor of T/MT/M into a compact latent 𝐙\mathbf{Z}. Each frame is represented by K+1K{+}1 tokens: the KK deformation tokens from the spatial VAE and one additional rigid token that embeds the pose (𝐑t\mathbf{R}_{t} and 𝐜t\mathbf{c}_{t}) in its channels. This token sequence first passes through axial blocks that alternate self-attention across tokens within a frame and along the temporal axis (Ho et al., 2019; Bertasius et al., 2021; Arnab et al., 2021), after which it is decoupled into a deformation track and a rigid track. For the deformation track, the standard choice (as in video VAEs) would merge every T/MT/M frames into one latent frame and then decode it with a local temporal upsampler. However, this standard design introduces the staircase artifacts analyzed in Sec. 4 (Staircase analysis). We instead employ a holistic temporal representation where time is summarized by factorized self-attention: for each of the KK spatial tokens separately, MM learnable queries are prepended to its temporal sequence, attended along the time axis, and kept as the only temporal outputs, giving K×MK\times M tokens in total, which we call holistic temporal tokens. For the rigid track, sharing the holistic tokens with the deformation causes capacity competition and degrades the reconstruction (see ablation in Sec. 4.1). The rigid token therefore takes a dedicated linear temporal pathway and recombines with the canonical shape per frame during decoding. Ultimately, the two tracks merge into the single joint latent 𝐙\mathbf{Z} that serves as the training target of the LDM. The ST-VAE decoder is kept frozen during the LDM stage to decode latents back into full trajectories.

LDM. Conditioned on the initial state, the LDM predicts the latent of the full TT-frame trajectory in one pass. The frame-00 mesh is injected via cross-attention on its spatial latent, while the pose, the initial velocity, and the stiffness condition the network via adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN) alongside the flow timestep. The mesh topology enters only through the frozen decoder, whose graph neural network (GNN) refines the decoded vertices over the tetrahedral mesh. We employ a flow-matching (Lipman et al., 2023) diffusion transformer (DiT) (Peebles and Xie, 2023) utilizing rectified flow (Liu et al., 2023) to model the probability path. Architecture details are in Appendix A.

3.3 Training

Our model is trained in three stages. The first stage trains the spatial VAE with a Charbonnier (smoothed L1L_{1}) position-reconstruction loss and a Kullback–Leibler (KL) loss (see the spatial-VAE-pretraining ablation in Appendix F). The second stage trains the ST-VAE on top of the pretrained spatial VAE. Its loss consists mainly of deformation and rigid reconstruction losses over all TT frames and a KL loss, together with a latent-anchor loss to the spatial manifold. The third stage trains the LDM on the pretrained, frozen ST-VAE, with a flow-matching velocity mean-squared error (MSE) loss. Complete loss forms, weights, and training details are given in Appendix A.

Constitutive-Model-Free Supervision. Notably, our framework relies entirely on kinematic supervision. Every reconstruction loss is computed directly from geometry, namely vertex positions, velocities, and rigid poses. No constitutive models are used during training or inference. This purely data-driven approach makes PhysLDM agnostic to the underlying simulator’s energy model, allowing it to seamlessly scale across diverse materials, and giving it the potential to learn from real-world captured trajectories where explicit energy models are unavailable (Appendix M).

4 Experiments

Data and setup.

We generate high-accuracy physical simulation data with a GPU FEM solver based on IPC (Huang et al., 2024a; Huang et al., 2025). For each scene, we randomly select nn objects (n≤3n\leq 3) from more than 30,00030{,}000 Objaverse objects, tetrahedralize them with fTetWild (Hu et al., 2020) into volumetric meshes, and assign each object a random initial velocity (v0v_{0}) and a random stiffness (Young’s modulus, EE). The simulation time step is 1/601/60 s and each trajectory has 6464 frames. The Objaverse scenes (63,39763{,}397 single-object and 16,07816{,}078 multi-body trajectories) are split into training, validation, and held-out test sets at a ratio of 90%:5%:5%90\%:5\%:5\%. For OOD evaluation, we generate scenes in the same way from the objects of two other datasets, GSO and Toys4K. The ST-VAE and the LDM are trained on scenes with N∈[500,5,000]N\in[500,5{,}000] vertices. The ST-VAE and LDM results in this paper are trained on single-object scenes (n=1n{=}1). Our extended model is trained on multi-object scenes (n≤3n\leq 3; see the multi-body extension in Appendix J). In the controlled ST-VAE comparisons, we use ST-VAE Small (K=512K{=}512, T=32T{=}32, M=4M{=}4, 9595M parameters). In the LDM experiments, we use ST-VAE Base (K=512K{=}512, T=64T{=}64, M=8M{=}8, 124124M parameters; Table 3). Both configurations compress a trajectory by 8​N/5138N/513 in token count, which reaches 78×78\times at the 5,0005{,}000-vertex cap. Training details are in Appendix A. Full data details, evaluation setup, and metric definitions are in Appendix B.

Staircase analysis.

Standard temporal compression methods (such as video VAEs) uniformly compress consecutive frames into fixed latent blocks along the time axis and decode them with a local temporal upsampler, but this approach is not suitable for 3D volumetric deformable dynamics trajectory reconstruction: it causes the object’s deformation to hold and then snap to the next state, creating an unnatural “staircase” artifact that severely degrades visual fidelity. While this timing error is easily perceptible in video playback, it is difficult to identify from static multi-frame snapshots alone; therefore, we quantify it via the deformation-change correlation (DCC), defined in Appendix B.3. Although DCC does not solely measure overall reconstruction quality on its own, it plays a decisive role in evaluating the physical plausibility of the motion when reconstruction precision is comparable. A detailed analysis of the staircase artifact is given in Appendix C.

Chaos analysis.

Although physics simulators are commonly assumed to produce deterministic trajectories once initial states and parameters are fully specified, this is not guaranteed for GPU solvers. As shown in Fig. 7, running the same scene five times from byte-identical inputs yields visibly different final poses, with corresponding vertices landing up to 442442 mm apart. This divergence stems from two factors: first, the underlying hardware non-determinism of GPU solvers introduces negligible initial variations; second, the inherently chaotic nature of complex deformable dynamics can rapidly amplify these microscopic errors into macroscopic trajectory divergence. Consequently, training data is not a deterministic function of initial conditions. We also verify this at scale on the 300300 Objaverse held-out scenes: running each scene twice from identical initial conditions, the final-frame vertex trajectories of 23.7%23.7\% of these meter-scale scenes differ by more than 1%1\% of the object size (about 11 cm), and those of 7.7%7.7\% differ by more than 5%5\% (about 55 cm) (Table 5). This chaotic nature suggests why regression models struggle: faced with multiple branching futures, a squared-error loss would drive the model toward the conditional mean, collapsing incompatible outcomes into a damped and non-physical average. A generative approach like our LDM naturally avoids this by sampling plausible trajectories. A more detailed chaos analysis is given in Appendix D.

ST-VAE Reconstruction Results.

Table 1 and Fig. 3 evaluate our holistic ST-VAE against two alternative designs: standard temporal compression (the design of video VAEs) and a direct world-coordinate baseline (which applies holistic compression without the factoring of Eq. (1)). All models share a matched compression rate and are assessed across the same three evaluation sets (Appendix E). The results yield three primary observations. First, holistic temporal compression eliminates staircase artifacts. Standard compression suffers from the staircase artifact (Sec. 4, Staircase analysis), which shows up as its clearly lower DCC. Our holistic ST-VAE preserves accurate motion timing, achieving a DCC exceeding 0.930.93 across all evaluation sets. Furthermore, augmenting the standard baseline with auxiliary velocity or spectral losses, or placing the latent frames adaptively in time, does not mitigate this limitation (Table 7). Second, decoupling rigid motion from deformation enhances precision. The direct world-coordinate baseline underperforms the holistic ST-VAE across all deformation and rigid motion metrics, and shows noisy and cluttered geometric detail in the visual comparison (Fig. 3). Third, the holistic ST-VAE achieves superior precision across diverse scenarios. Under up to 78×78\times compression, the ST-VAE yields a mean geometric reconstruction error of just 2.482.48 mm on held-out scenes, representing about half the error of the standard baseline, with a median vertex error below 22 mm. It achieves the best performance across nearly all metrics and datasets, except for one rigid-rotation entry where it is a close second. This performance holds robustly zero-shot on OOD sets like GSO and Toys4K, where its errors stay at the same level as in distribution, and on high-resolution meshes exceeding the 5,0005{,}000-vertex training cap, where its mean error is still only a few millimeters. The least accurate held-out cases, geometries with many long, thin features, are analyzed in Appendix I.

Prediction Results.

Table 2 and Fig. 4 compare three models predicting a 6464-frame trajectory from the same initial state: our LDM, a capacity-matched deterministic regression model (both using one-shot prediction and the same ST-VAE), and a frame-by-frame AR graph network based on MeshGraphNets (MGN) (Appendix E.3). Because complex deformable dynamics are inherently chaotic, world-space error alone is insufficient to evaluate prediction quality, as the ground truth represents only one of many valid outcomes. Therefore, Table 2 primarily relies on physics-consistency checks (Appendix B; the full set of checks is in Table 8). Across all metrics and datasets, the LDM significantly outperforms both baselines. We highlight three observations from the results. First, the LDM consistently outperforms deterministic regression in generating physically plausible trajectories. The regression model produces damped outputs with geometric artifacts and jitter (e.g., 22.7%22.7\% volume violations versus 7.9%7.9\% for the LDM on held-out scenes). In contrast, the LDM reduces these artifacts and better preserves the deformation-to-rigid energy ratio. Second, one-shot prediction provides the global temporal context necessary to prevent the compounding errors typically seen in autoregressive models. Consequently, the AR baseline drifts over time and accumulates nearly three times the world-space error of the LDM (80.680.6 against 28.228.2 mm). Third, this strong performance transfers zero-shot to OOD datasets (GSO and Toys4K), demonstrating the robust generalization of our approach. Finally, the LDM remains highly efficient, running at 4040 to 8080 frames per second on a single GPU, even for high-resolution meshes exceeding the training cap (Appendix G).

The diffusion results in Table 2 use a single sample per scene, which cannot show whether diffusion captures the several possible outcomes of a chaotic scene. To test whether diffusion benefits from modeling several outcomes, we compare the two models separately on chaotic and non-chaotic held-out scenes and draw eight diffusion samples per scene (Appendix D.6). Diffusion outperforms regression on both subsets. One may worry that this only reflects a stronger model. However, the diffusion samples spread much more widely on the chaotic scenes, and this spread follows the difference between two runs of the solver. Since the model is the same on both subsets, this effect comes from the generative paradigm and not from a stronger model. A soft key dropped onto the ground illustrates it (Fig. 8). Run twice, the solver lets the key fall over in two different directions. Every diffusion sample faithfully falls toward one of the two correct directions, while regression predicts a non-physical average that matches neither run.

4.1 Ablations

ST-VAE.

We remove the ST-VAE and let a DiT of the same capacity as our LDM denoise the vertex×\timesframe tokens directly (Table 9). Without the latent, one-shot diffusion at native resolution is computationally prohibitive. Memory per sample grows with the vertex count. Even on a 140140 GiB H200, the model at batch 11 runs out of memory at 2,6002{,}600 vertices. With the latent, the LDM works on a fixed number of tokens and its cost is independent of the vertex count. The vertex-dependent cost moves to the ST-VAE stage, whose training memory grows linearly with NN (Table 9), so on the same GPU the training cap rises from about 2,5002{,}500 vertices without the latent to about 14,00014{,}000 for ST-VAE Base. The latent also improves the quality of the generated geometry. A raw-coordinate model predicts every vertex directly, so any noise left by the sampler shows up as per-vertex jitter. Our model decodes all vertices from the latent, so the same noise only shifts the shape slightly and coherently (illustrated in Appendix L).

The dedicated rigid pathway in ST-VAE.

In the ST-VAE (Sec. 3.2), the rigid token bypasses the holistic temporal compression and takes its own linear temporal pathway. To test this design, we route the rigid token through the shared holistic temporal compression instead. In our experiments, this one change causes two failures: the translation error explodes, and the reconstructed deformation shrinks drastically (detailed diagnostics in Appendix F). Further ablations (spatial-VAE pretraining and the decoder GNN) are reported in Appendix F.

4.2 Differentiable Applications

We demonstrate the end-to-end differentiability of PhysLDM on two tasks of increasing difficulty and compare against two differentiable simulators, DiffIPC (Huang et al., 2024b) and Newton/Warp (The Newton Contributors, 2025). The detailed comparison, together with the setup and results, is given in Appendix K.

Material Estimation.

The bottom-right block of Fig. 1 shows a material estimation task. Given a single simulated trajectory of a body with unknown stiffness, we recover its Young’s modulus EE by gradient descent through the model, since the mismatch to the observed trajectory is differentiable in EE end to end. Because Young’s modulus is usually measured on a logarithmic scale, we optimize EE in log10\log_{10} space, where an error of 11 dex means a factor of 1010. To cover a wide range of stiffness, we repeat the task on seven bodies with moduli from 3×1043\times 10^{4} to 3×1063\times 10^{6} Pa, each starting from an initial guess up to 1.11.1 dex away. In all seven cases, our model recovers EE within 0.060.06 dex in 4040 Adam steps, which takes about 4040 seconds per run. DiffIPC solves the task only after its solver parameters are tuned by hand, and then needs 2626 minutes on 4848 threads. Newton/Warp fails in the backward pass, because backpropagating through its enormous number of substeps explodes the gradient.

Beyond Material Estimation: Designing the Throw.

Based on the first task, we may ask a further question: which throw reveals the stiffness best, so that the estimation above becomes easier? Easier means that a change of EE produces a larger change of the trajectory, so the trajectory carries more information about the stiffness. We therefore maximize the sensitivity of the predicted trajectory to EE over the release velocity by gradient ascent through the model. The objective is a derivative, so its gradient is a second-order quantity. Our model supports higher-order derivatives through the automatic differentiation of PyTorch, so it provides this gradient directly, and 3030 Adam steps finish the design in 77 minutes. Replayed in the ground-truth simulator, the optimized throw makes the rigid motion 13×13\times more sensitive to the stiffness. DiffIPC offers only first-order derivatives and cannot be applied directly to this second-order task. A workaround is to obtain the second-order gradient by nested finite differences, but then DiffIPC is about 635×635\times slower than our model per gradient step. The whole design would take several days, which is not acceptable in practice. Newton/Warp does not produce a usable first-order gradient on this scene, so a second-order one is out of reach.

5 Conclusion

We introduce PhysLDM, a latent diffusion paradigm for predicting the dynamics of high-fidelity volumetric deformable bodies. To overcome the computational limits of processing high-resolution meshes, we developed a novel holistic ST-VAE that explicitly disentangles global rigid motion from local deformations. This architecture eliminates the staircase artifacts inherent to standard temporal compression, ensuring highly accurate trajectory reconstruction even for high-resolution, out-of-distribution meshes. Operating on this compact latent representation, we demonstrate that while deterministic regression produces damped, non-physical averages in this chaotic regime, our generative approach predicts physically consistent trajectories in a single diffusion pass. Finally, trained purely kinematically, PhysLDM delivers robust zero-shot generalization and provides end-to-end differentiability, unlocking complex inverse design optimizations that remain intractable for traditional solvers.

Limitations and Future Work. Currently, our model focuses on predicting 6464-frame trajectories in a single diffusion pass. Extending this one-shot approach into an autoregressive framework presents a promising direction for future research.
