Appendix A Architecture and Training Details

Our model is trained in three stages, one per component: the spatial VAE for 183183k iterations, ST-VAE Base for 150150k iterations, and the LDM for 278278k iterations. The three stages together take about 77 days on 88 H200 GPUs.

A.1 Stage 1: Spatial VAE

The spatial VAE is an 88-layer transformer of hidden width 512512 (4444M parameters). Its input is one frame in canonical coordinates, i.e. the rest shape plus the deformation 𝐝t\mathbf{d}_{t} of Eq. (1) with the rigid motion removed. The encoder cross-attends K=512K{=}512 learned query tokens against the NN vertex tokens of the frame and outputs KK latent tokens of width D=48D{=}48, independent of NN. We denote the latent of frame tt by 𝐳t\mathbf{z}_{t}. The decoder mirrors the encoder: the NN rest vertices, embedded with their positions, cross-attend the latent tokens and are decoded back to their NN displacements. The decoder additionally takes the mesh topology as input, because a shallow GNN over the tetrahedral mesh then refines the decoded displacements. The spatial VAE is trained first with a Charbonnier position loss and a KL term.

A.2 Stage 2: ST-VAE

The per-frame latents {𝐳t}t=1T\{\mathbf{z}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} are processed by a stack of factorized space–time attention blocks (Ho et al., 2019; Bertasius et al., 2021; Arnab et al., 2021). The holistic temporal compression then summarizes the time axis: MM learned query tokens attend over each spatial token’s TT-frame sequence, and only these MM outputs are kept as the temporal representation, while the TT per-frame outputs are discarded. The rigid-motion token bypasses this attention compression and is compressed by a separate linear temporal path. The two are kept apart because the rigid signal is orders of magnitude larger than the deformation and, when the two share one compression path, takes over the shared latent and starves the deformation track (Sec. 4.1, Appendix F). The two tracks then merge: the joint latent is 𝐙∈ℝM×(K+1)×D\mathbf{Z}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times(K+1)\times D} of Sec. 3.2, i.e. MM temporal tokens for each of the KK deformation tokens and the rigid token, each of width D=48D{=}48. The decoder mirrors the encoder: per-frame queries attend over the MM temporal tokens to recover a latent for every frame, which the spatial VAE decoder turns into vertex positions. Table 3 lists the two ST-VAE configurations used in this paper, ST-VAE Small for the controlled comparisons of Table 1 and ST-VAE Base for the LDM experiments (Sec. 4). Both configurations compress a trajectory by the same factor, counted in tokens. The input has one token per vertex per frame, T×NT\times N tokens in total, and the latent has M×(K+1)M\times(K{+}1) tokens. Since T/M=8T/M{=}8 and K+1=513K{+}1{=}513 in both configurations, the token compression ratio is 8​N/5138N/513, which reaches 78×78\times at the 5,0005{,}000-vertex cap.

A.3 Stage 3: LDM

The LDM and the regression model receive the same conditioning: the frame-00 spatial latent through cross-attention, and the initial pose, the initial velocity v0v_{0}, and the Young’s modulus EE through adaptive layer normalization. The LDM is a DiT with 1212 blocks of width 768768 (170170M parameters) operating on the 4,1044{,}104 latent tokens of ST-VAE Base (M×(K+1)=8×513M\times(K{+}1)=8\times 513 tokens of width D=48D{=}48). It is trained with rectified flow and sampled by Euler integration. The regression model is a capacity-matched transformer that emits the full latent trajectory in one pass. Training the spatial VAE, ST-VAE Base, and the LDM takes about 77 days in total on 88 H200 GPUs.

A.4 Loss details

All position losses use a Charbonnier penalty on the per-vertex error norm,

ℒcharb​(𝐱^,𝐱)=1|V|​∑i∈V∥𝐱^i−𝐱i∥2+ϵ2,ϵ=10−3(=1​mm),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{charb}}(\hat{\mathbf{x}},\mathbf{x})\;=\;\frac{1}{|V|}\sum_{i\in V}\sqrt{\lVert\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{i}-\mathbf{x}_{i}\rVert^{2}+\epsilon^{2}},\qquad\epsilon=10^{-3}\ (=1\,\mathrm{mm}), (2)

Stage 1: Spatial VAE. ℒS1=ℒcharb+β1​ℒKL\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{S1}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{charb}}+\beta_{1}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KL}} with a standard Gaussian KL term and β1=10−5\beta_{1}=10^{-5}.

Stage 2: ST-VAE. The objective combines the deformation reconstruction of all TT frames, the rigid track, and a KL term:

ℒS2=∑j∈{deform,R,c}(12​e−sj​ℒj+12​sj)+β2​ℒKLfb,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{S2}}=\sum_{j\in\{\mathrm{deform},R,c\}}\Big(\tfrac{1}{2}e^{-s_{j}}\mathcal{L}_{j}+\tfrac{1}{2}s_{j}\Big)+\beta_{2}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KL}}^{\mathrm{fb}}, (3)

where ℒdeform\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{deform}} is ℒcharb\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{charb}} averaged over the TT decoded frames, ℒR\mathcal{L}_{R} and ℒc\mathcal{L}_{c} are mean-squared errors on the rigid token’s rotation and translation, and the three are balanced by the learned uncertainty weights sjs_{j} of Kendall et al. (2018). ℒKLfb\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KL}}^{\mathrm{fb}} is the KL term with per-channel free bits (Kingma et al., 2016).

Stage 3: LDM. The latent is standardized per modality (rigid and deformation channels separately). With flow time τ\tau, noise ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}) and the straight path 𝐱τ=(1−τ)​𝐳+τ​ϵ\mathbf{x}_{\tau}=(1{-}\tau)\mathbf{z}+\tau\boldsymbol{\epsilon}, the LDM minimizes a token-weighted velocity regression

ℒDiT=𝔼τ,ϵ​[⟨wk​∥𝐯^k−(ϵ−𝐳)k∥2⟩k],wk={λrigidk​a rigid tokenλdeformotherwise,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DiT}}=\mathbb{E}_{\tau,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\Big[\big\langle w_{k}\,\lVert\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{k}-(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\mathbf{z})_{k}\rVert^{2}\big\rangle_{k}\Big],\qquad w_{k}=\begin{cases}\lambda_{\mathrm{rigid}}&k\ \text{a rigid token}\\ \lambda_{\mathrm{deform}}&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} (4)

where kk indexes the (K+1)×M(K{+}1)\times M latent tokens and λrigid\lambda_{\mathrm{rigid}} is a hand-tuned weight that up-weights the rigid token relative to the deformation tokens (λdeform=1\lambda_{\mathrm{deform}}{=}1). The regression model minimizes the same token-weighted mean-squared error directly on the latent.

Appendix B Data, Evaluation Setup, and Metrics

B.1 Data details

All simulation data are generated with StiffGIPC (Huang et al., 2025), a GPU IPC solver. IPC solvers are widely adopted in scenarios that demand high simulation accuracy, such as embodied AI (Kim et al., 2022; Li et al., 2025). Such a solver runs offline. Learning its behavior and turning it into a fast, fully differentiable neural simulator is therefore of practical importance. All 3D meshes used for training come from the Objaverse dataset (Deitke et al., 2023). Each asset is voxel-remeshed to a watertight surface, tetrahedralized with fTetWild (Hu et al., 2020), reduced to its largest connected component, and rescaled to a unit bounding box. Meshes with more than 10,00010{,}000 vertices are discarded, and the ST-VAE and the LDM are trained on scenes with 500500–5,0005{,}000 vertices. Every scene drops one meter-scale solid onto a ground plane. The object is released with its lowest point 0.850.85 to 1.651.65 m above the ground. Each object receives a random initial velocity v0v_{0} and a random stiffness EE (a horizontal v0∼U⁡(0,2)v_{0}\sim U(0,2) m/s and a Young’s modulus EE log-uniform in [3×104,3×106][3\times 10^{4},3\times 10^{6}] Pa) under a Stable Neo-Hookean material. Multi-body scenes follow the same setting with two or three objects, each with its own EE and v0v_{0}, thrown toward each other so that they collide in mid-air before reaching the ground. In total, the dataset contains 63,39763{,}397 single-object and 16,07816{,}078 multi-body simulated trajectories. The simulation time step is 1/601/60 s, and each trajectory has 6464 frames. Held-out scenes are excluded from all three training stages, and every reported number is computed on these held-out scenes or on the OOD sets. For OOD evaluation we generate 1,0151{,}015 GSO and 3,8143{,}814 Toys4K scenes under the identical simulation setting. They never appear in training.

B.2 Evaluation setup

(a) ST-VAE reconstruction (Table 1). For each evaluation set (held-out, GSO, Toys4K), we randomly draw 300300 scenes with 500≤N≤5,000500\leq N\leq 5{,}000 vertices for the main columns and 300300 scenes with N>5,000N>5{,}000 vertices for the large-mesh columns. Every model is evaluated on the same scenes. (b) Prediction (Table 2). The same 300300 scenes per set within 500≤N≤5,000500\leq N\leq 5{,}000. The LDM uses 5050 Euler steps. Every metric is a per-scene value, reported as the median across scenes to limit the influence of a few extreme values.

B.3 Metrics of Table 1

  • •

    DCC (deformation-change correlation): the deformation change of a trajectory at frame tt is the mean vertex displacement between two consecutive frames in canonical (rigid-free) coordinates, v⁡(t)=meanv​∥𝐝t+1,v−𝐝t,v∥v(t)=\mathrm{mean}_{v}\lVert\mathbf{d}_{t+1,v}-\mathbf{d}_{t,v}\rVert, where 𝐝t,v\mathbf{d}_{t,v} is the position of vertex vv in the deformation field 𝐝t\mathbf{d}_{t}. The deformation-change curve is v⁡(t)v(t) over the trajectory. DCC is the Pearson correlation between the deformation-change curves of the reconstruction and of the ground truth. It is reported as the mean across scenes. It detects the staircase artifact directly, since holds suppress the speed and snaps spike it. This metric is amplitude-invariant, so it does not reflect reconstruction quality on its own and should be considered together with the other metrics.

  • •

    Recon (geometric reconstruction error; mean / med / P90): the encode–decode error of the deformation field, i.e. the per-vertex Euclidean error of the rigid-free deformation 𝐝t\mathbf{d}_{t} averaged over vertices and frames of a scene (mm). The three columns are the mean, median, and 90th percentile across scenes. The 90th percentile reflects the hardest 10%10\% of scenes. For the direct world-coordinate baseline, which has no deformation field of its own, a rigid transform is fitted to each output frame by the Kabsch algorithm, and the residual after removing it is scored as the deformation error.

  • •

    rot (rotation error): the geodesic SO⁡(3)\mathrm{SO}(3) distance between the predicted and ground-truth per-frame rotation (relative to frame 00), averaged over the frames of a scene and then over scenes (degrees). For the direct world-coordinate baseline, the rotation and translation are those of the per-frame fitted rigid transform.

  • •

    trans (translation error): the centroid translation error (relative to frame 00), averaged over frames and then over scenes (mm).

B.4 Metrics of Table 2

All of these metrics are computed from the predicted and ground-truth trajectories alone and do not require knowledge of the underlying constitutive model. The violation rates are defined as follows. A physical quantity (speed or acceleration) is computed for every vertex at every frame, once from the prediction and once from the ground truth. Each such vertex-frame pair is one sample. A sample is counted as a violation if the predicted value is more than twice, or less than half, the ground-truth value. The violation rate is the fraction of violated samples. Samples whose ground-truth value is too small to be meaningful are excluded by a magnitude threshold.

  • •

    Volume viol. (volume violation rate): this measures whether the prediction preserves volume where the ground truth does. For every tetrahedron at every frame, we compute how much its volume differs from its rest volume, once in the ground truth and once in the prediction. We look only at the cases where the ground truth changes the volume by less than 3%3\%, because there the ground truth preserves volume. Among these cases, a violation is one where the prediction changes the volume by more than 10%10\%. The rate is the fraction of violations.

  • •

    Self-int. (self-intersection rate): the percentage of surface triangles of the tetrahedral mesh that cross another surface triangle, averaged over frames and reported as the median across scenes. The ground truth has no self-intersection in any frame, so its value is 00.

  • •

    Vel. viol. and Acc. viol. (velocity and acceleration violation rates): the violation rate of the per-vertex speed and acceleration magnitudes. The acceleration threshold excludes free fall and settled frames.

  • •

    K​Edef/K​ErigKE_{\mathrm{def}}/KE_{\mathrm{rig}} (deformation-to-rigid kinetic energy ratio): a rigid transform (𝐑t,𝐜t)(\mathbf{R}_{t},\mathbf{c}_{t}) is fitted to every frame by the Kabsch algorithm, which gives the rigid trajectory 𝐫t,v=𝐑t​𝐱¯v+𝐜t\mathbf{r}_{t,v}=\mathbf{R}_{t}\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{v}+\mathbf{c}_{t} of the rest shape 𝐱¯\bar{\mathbf{x}}. The vertex velocity 𝐯t,v\mathbf{v}_{t,v} (central difference of 𝐱t,v\mathbf{x}_{t,v}) is split into the rigid velocity 𝐯t,vrig\mathbf{v}^{\mathrm{rig}}_{t,v} (central difference of 𝐫t,v\mathbf{r}_{t,v}) and the deformation residual 𝐯t,vdef=𝐯t,v−𝐯t,vrig\mathbf{v}^{\mathrm{def}}_{t,v}=\mathbf{v}_{t,v}-\mathbf{v}^{\mathrm{rig}}_{t,v}. With lumped vertex masses mvm_{v} and the impact window WW (±10\pm 10 frames around first contact), the two kinetic energies are

    K​Edef=12​∑t∈W∑vmv​∥𝐯t,vdef∥2,K​Erig=12​∑t∈W∑vmv​∥𝐯t,vrig∥2,KE_{\mathrm{def}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{t\in W}\sum_{v}m_{v}\lVert\mathbf{v}^{\mathrm{def}}_{t,v}\rVert^{2},\qquad KE_{\mathrm{rig}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{t\in W}\sum_{v}m_{v}\lVert\mathbf{v}^{\mathrm{rig}}_{t,v}\rVert^{2},

    and the reported value is (K​Edef/K​Erig)pred/(K​Edef/K​Erig)GT(KE_{\mathrm{def}}/KE_{\mathrm{rig}})_{\mathrm{pred}}\,/\,(KE_{\mathrm{def}}/KE_{\mathrm{rig}})_{\mathrm{GT}}, taken as the median across scenes. Scenes where the ground truth barely deforms (deformation below 1%1\% of the kinetic energy) are skipped. At impact, the kinetic energy of the object is divided between the motion of the object as a whole and the internal motion that deforms it. How much goes into deformation depends on how soft the object is and how hard it hits. The ground truth gives the correct proportion for the same object and the same impact, so comparing the two ratios shows whether the prediction moves energy into deformation the way the GPU solver does. A value below 11 means the prediction deforms less than the ground truth and moves more rigidly. A value above 11 would mean unphysical deformation or jitter. In Table 2 every model is below 11, and the regression model is the lowest on all three evaluation sets, consistent with the damped averages discussed in Sec. 4.

  • •

    World err (world-coordinate error): the per-vertex Euclidean error in world coordinates against the ground-truth trajectory, averaged over vertices and frames, reported as the median across scenes (mm). Because deformable dynamics are chaotic, the ground truth may be only one of many possible outcomes, so this number is a reference and not a full measure of prediction quality.

Appendix C Staircase Analysis Details

This section diagnoses the staircase artifact. It appears in four baselines of Table 7: the standard baseline, its two variants (velocity loss and spectral loss), and adaptive compression. The architectures of these baselines are described in Appendix E.1.

C.1 Symptom and diagnosis

The symptom is wrong timing of rapid motion. Where the ground truth changes quickly, for instance at impact, the reconstruction holds its shape for several frames and then jumps to catch up, so the motion arrives late and all at once. We diagnose it in three ways. Fig. 5 plots the deformation-change curve on five scenes. The curves of the standard baseline, its two variants, and adaptive compression stay below ground truth for several frames and then overshoot it in one frame. The holistic ST-VAE follows the ground truth, and so does the direct world-coordinate baseline, which uses the same holistic temporal compression. Fig. 6 shows the same behavior directly on the silhouettes of one scene. The silhouettes of the standard baseline and its variants change less than the ground truth for three frames and then more than it in the last one or two frames. Adaptive compression changes less than the ground truth over all five frame pairs and releases the motion even later. The direct world-coordinate baseline follows the ground truth until the last pair. Table 4 scores the five scenes with DCC. The holistic ST-VAE is the best or tied on every scene.

C.2 Cause

In the standard baseline, the decoded frames at the latent-frame positions are accurate, and the frames between them carry the error. The most likely cause is that standard compression summarizes every kk frames into one latent frame and loses the high-frequency temporal information that says when, within those kk frames, the rapid change happens. One might think that the problem is a mismatch between neighboring blocks. This is not the case. Two observations show that the error builds up inside each block. First, the standard baseline moves too little during the early frames of every block and then catches up in the last frames, whereas the ground truth moves at a steady pace throughout the block. Second, smoothing the reconstruction across block boundaries does not remove the artifact.

C.3 Why the variants and adaptive compression do not help

The two variants of the standard baseline and the adaptive-compression baseline all keep the approach of standard temporal compression: they compress the trajectory into a fixed number of latent frames and then reconstruct the frames by local temporal upsampling, so they leave the artifact in place. The velocity loss and the spectral loss change the training signal only. The standard baseline still cannot place the rapid change at the right instant between two latent frames. Adaptive compression moves the latent frames toward the impact, which makes the steps fewer but steeper. A likely reason is that the rebound and settling phases are left with one or two latent frames, so their motion is released in a late snap. The direct world-coordinate baseline uses the holistic temporal compression and shows almost no staircase. Its high DCC in Table 4 together with its lower precision in Table 1 shows that its weakness is precision rather than timing.

Appendix D Chaos in Traditional GPU Simulators

This section gives the details of the chaos experiment in Sec. 4 (Chaos analysis). A common assumption is that a physics simulator produces a deterministic trajectory once the initial state and parameters are fully specified. In practice, this is not guaranteed for modern GPU solvers. Because of their speed, GPU solvers are increasingly used to generate physical simulation data at scale, so the consequences of this non-determinism for learning deserve a closer look. Two separate facts are involved. First, a GPU solver is not bit-reproducible: its parallel reductions add floating-point numbers in a different order on every run, which perturbs the state at the level of rounding error. On its own this would be harmless. Second, the complex dynamics of deformable bodies are chaotic: it can amplify such a perturbation into a macroscopic difference in the outcome. The experiment below separates the two.

D.1 Setup

We take one held-out scene, a soft tennis racket dropped onto the ground, and run the GPU solver five times on the same GPU from byte-identical inputs: the same tetrahedral mesh, initial state, material parameters, and solver configuration. To measure how far two runs drift apart at a given frame, we compute the displacement of every vertex between the two runs and report the largest one as a fraction of the object’s extent.

D.2 The perturbation is tiny

The non-determinism of the solver is real but minute. After the first simulation step the five runs differ by at most 0.020.02 mm, two hundred-thousandths of the object size. Before the racket reaches the ground, the runs still differ by at most 3%3\% of the object size, mostly in the strings of the net, and their centres of mass by less than 11 mm. Until the racket reaches the ground, the five runs are therefore practically identical.

D.3 Amplification after impact

The behavior changes qualitatively at impact. After the racket hits the ground, the runs diverge rapidly and settle into visibly different poses (Fig. 7). Over the ten pairs of runs, the final divergence ranges from 10%10\% to 51%51\% of the object size, with a median of 21%21\%. The same vertex can land up to 442442 mm apart in two runs.

To check that this is chaos and not a peculiarity of the reduction order, we replace the rounding noise by a controlled perturbation: a deterministic initial rotation of the racket between 10−810^{-8} and 10−210^{-2} rad. The final divergence is of the same order for every magnitude and does not grow with it. A perturbation a million times larger does not produce a larger difference. This is the signature of chaotic dynamics. The racket has several possible resting poses. Even the smallest perturbation is already enough to change which one it ends in, so making the perturbation larger does not make the difference larger. It only changes which resting pose the racket lands in.

D.4 Where the chaos comes from

The sensitivity comes from complex dynamics involving contact. When the racket hits the ground, the solver makes a discrete decision about which edge or corner touches first, and a microscopic perturbation can flip this decision. From then on the bounce and the final pose follow different paths. In our experiments, soft objects that are thin, branchy, or non-convex are more prone to amplifying this chaotic effect.

D.5 How common is chaos across scenes?

The racket above is a single scene. To measure how often two runs of the solver diverge, we run the GPU solver a second time from byte-identical inputs on all 300300 Objaverse held-out scenes of Table 1 and compare the two runs. We measure their difference relative to the object size, defined as the diagonal of the bounding box at frame 00. Table 5 counts the scenes whose difference exceeds 1%1\%, 5%5\%, and 10%10\% of the object size, using either the mean per-vertex error over the whole trajectory or the per-vertex error at the last frame.

Most scenes are reproduced closely. The median difference between the two runs is 0.50.5 mm over the trajectory and 1.01.0 mm at the last frame. A substantial minority of scenes, however, diverge. At the last frame, about a quarter of the scenes end more than 1%1\% of the object size apart, and the most divergent scene ends 35%35\% apart. In all of these scenes, the two runs agree to sub-millimeter precision until ground contact and separate afterwards, as in the racket example. A difference of 1%1\% of the object size means that the two runs end more than 11 cm apart on a meter-scale object, which is already a large error for high-precision physical simulation. A regression model can only learn the mean of such diverging outcomes, so high precision is difficult to reach on these scenes.

D.6 Regression versus diffusion on chaotic and non-chaotic scenes

In a chaotic scene, the same initial state can lead to several different outcomes. A regression model gives one prediction per initial state, while a diffusion model can draw several. This section tests whether, on chaotic scenes, the samples of the LDM actually cover the different outcomes that the solver produces. We split the 300300 held-out scenes of Table 5 by how far the two solver runs end apart: 7171 chaotic scenes, whose runs end more than 1%1\% of the object size apart, and 229229 non-chaotic scenes. For every scene we draw eight samples from the LDM and report two numbers: the error of a single sample, and the error of the best of the eight samples. Choosing the best sample needs the ground truth, so the best-of-eight result is an upper bound on sample selection, not a usable predictor. All other settings follow Table 2.

Diffusion outperforms regression on both subsets. Table 6 shows that a single diffusion sample already improves on the regression model in every metric, on both subsets. It has a lower error than the regression model in 79%79\% of the non-chaotic scenes and 65%65\% of the chaotic scenes. The advantage of diffusion is therefore not limited to chaotic scenes.

Multiple samples matter more under chaos. What differs between the two subsets is how much the eight samples add over a single one. Picking the best of the eight lowers the median error by 3.43.4 mm on the non-chaotic scenes and by 9.39.3 mm on the chaotic scenes. The samples also spread further apart under chaos: the gap between the best and the worst sample of a scene is 77 mm on the non-chaotic scenes and 2525 mm on the chaotic scenes (medians over scenes). On the chaotic scenes, this spread follows the physics. It grows with the distance between the two solver runs (Spearman ρ=0.38\rho=0.38, p=0.001p=0.001), and the second solver run lies inside the spread of the eight samples in 99%99\% of the scenes. The benefit does not depend on picking the best sample: averaged over the eight samples, the median final-frame error on the chaotic scenes is 138138 mm, below the 162162 mm of the regression model. The diffusion model is thus more uncertain where the physics is less predictable, and this uncertainty covers outcomes that the solver itself produces.

An example: a falling soft key. In a scene with several possible outcomes, diffusion can learn these outcomes, whereas regression can only learn a non-physical average that matches none of them. Fig. 8 shows such a scene, a soft key. When the solver is run twice, the key falls over in two different directions. The regression model predicts a single pose that lies between the two runs and resembles neither. The eight diffusion samples instead fall on both sides, and the closest of them come close to each of the two runs. Other scenes behave similarly. Among the six scenes whose two runs end more than 30∘30^{\circ} apart, at least one diffusion sample ends within 30∘30^{\circ} of a solver run in five scenes, while the regression model does so in only one.

An advantage of the paradigm, not of a stronger model. One may worry that the diffusion model is simply the stronger model (the LDM uses 5050 sampling steps, the regression model a single pass), and that the results above reflect this difference. Three observations show that on chaotic scenes the advantage comes from the paradigm. First, the diffusion samples differ from each other in a way that follows the physics: their spread grows with the distance between the two solver runs and contains the second run in 99%99\% of the chaotic scenes. A deterministic model, however strong, gives a single prediction per initial state and has no such spread. Second, where the solver itself produces clearly different outcomes, the diffusion samples reach them, while the regression prediction is a non-physical average between them, as in the key example. Third, the benefit of drawing several samples depends on the scenes, not on the model. With the same model on both subsets, it is almost three times larger on the chaotic scenes (9.39.3 against 3.43.4 mm), whereas a difference in model strength would affect both subsets alike.

In summary, diffusion predicts more accurately than regression on both chaotic and non-chaotic scenes. On chaotic scenes it also produces several plausible outcomes, while regression gives a single non-physical average result. These results show that diffusion is better suited to chaotic deformable dynamics.

Appendix E Baselines

This section describes the baselines of Table 1 and Table 2, and reports the full reconstruction and prediction results (Tables 7 and 8). The reconstruction baselines are alternative learned representations of the same trajectories, and the prediction baselines are alternative dynamics models started from the same initial state.

E.1 Reconstruction baselines (Tables 1 and 7)

All reconstruction baselines use the 8×8\times temporal compression rate and the T=32T{=}32 window of ST-VAE Small, start from the same pretrained spatial VAE (except the direct world-coordinate baseline), and are trained on the same data with comparable budgets.

  • •

    Standard: standard temporal compression of video VAEs. It stacks per-frame latents {𝐳t}t=1T\{\mathbf{z}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} and shares the factorized spatiotemporal attention of our ST-VAE, but downsamples time by strided convolution to Tlat=T/kT_{\mathrm{lat}}=T/k latent frames and reconstructs the full frame rate from this time-ordered sequence of latent frames with a local temporal upsampler.

  • •

    + velocity loss: the strongest variant of the standard baseline we found. It adds a velocity-matching loss on the consecutive-frame differences of the reconstructed deformation and an unfrozen spatial VAE.

  • •

    + spectral loss: the standard baseline with an additional loss on the deformation-change curve of Appendix B.3. The curve is transformed along the time axis with a Fourier transform, and the energy at each frequency is compared with that of the ground-truth curve. Low frequencies correspond to slow changes of the deformation and high frequencies to fast ones, so the loss asks the reconstruction to contain as much fast change as the ground truth instead of smoothing it away. It fails possibly because a frequency spectrum records how much fast change there is but not when it happens, so the standard baseline still cannot place the rapid change at the right instant between two latent frames.

  • •

    Adaptive compression: a separate baseline that keeps the number of latent frames of the standard baseline but places them non-uniformly along time according to the temporal curvature of the ground-truth deformation. Its lower DCC in Table 1 may have the following cause. With only M=4M{=}4 latent frames per 3232-frame window, the impact takes most of them and the rebound and settling frames are left with one or two, so their motion is likely reconstructed flat and released in a late snap.

  • •

    Direct world-coord. (direct world-coordinate reconstruction): removes the factoring of Eq. (1). Its spatial VAE is trained on world-coordinate frames without canonicalization, and the same holistic temporal compression is applied on top without a rigid token, so rigid motion and deformation share one latent.

E.2 Full reconstruction results (Table 7)

Table 7 reports the full ST-VAE reconstruction comparison with all six ST-VAEs, including the two variants of the standard baseline and the adaptive-compression baseline, which are omitted from Table 1.

E.3 Prediction baselines (Table 2)

The prediction baselines receive the same initial state as PhysLDM.

  • •

    Regression: a deterministic regression model that is capacity-matched to the LDM and shares its ST-VAE and conditioning. It is a transformer that emits the full latent trajectory in one pass and is trained with the token-weighted mean-squared error of Appendix A, so that only the predictive paradigm differs between the two.

  • •

    MGN-style AR (MeshGraphNets-style autoregressive model): a graph network (Pfaff et al., 2021) over the tetrahedral mesh graph that predicts one frame at a time from the previous frames, with the noise-injected one-step training standard in that family (Sanchez-Gonzalez et al., 2020), retrained on our scenes. Predicting world coordinates step by step, it accumulates error over time and drifts far from the ground truth (Table 2). It is compared with our model under a fair setting.

E.4 Full prediction results (Table 8)

Table 8 reports the prediction comparison with all six physics checks, including the velocity and acceleration violation rates that are omitted from Table 2, together with the ST-VAE reconstruction of the ground truth as a reference row, which gives the autoencoder’s own contribution to each metric.

Appendix F More Ablations

This section collects the ablations that support design choices of the model: the use of the ST-VAE, the dedicated rigid pathway, the spatial-VAE pretraining, and the decoder GNN.

F.1 The ST-VAE

This section gives the measurements behind the ST-VAE ablation of Sec. 4.1, which asks what happens to the training cost when the ST-VAE is removed and the LDM denoises the raw vertex×\timesframe tokens directly. We compare two options on the same GPU at increasing vertex counts NN. The first is our LDM architecture applied to the raw tokens, without any latent. The second is our pipeline with the ST-VAE, where the LDM works on a fixed set of 4,1044{,}104 latent tokens and the ST-VAE is the stage with the largest memory footprint. Table 9 lists the peak training memory of both.

Without the ST-VAE the number of tokens is T×NT\times N, so memory grows with NN. The raw-token model fits at batch 11 up to 2,5002{,}500 vertices and runs out of memory at 2,6002{,}600, below the median resolution of our dataset (∼3,400{\sim}3{,}400 vertices). More than half of the training scenes therefore cannot be processed at all. With the ST-VAE, the LDM costs about 4.44.4 GiB per trajectory at any NN. The ST-VAE stage grows linearly with NN, by about 88 GiB per 1,0001{,}000 vertices, and ST-VAE Base trains up to about 14,00014{,}000 vertices on the same card. The latent therefore does not remove the vertex-dependent cost, but moves it to a stage that scales far more gently.

F.2 The rigid pathway

Sec. 4.1 shows that routing the rigid token through the shared holistic temporal compression makes the translation error explode and starves the deformation track: on a small held-out diagnostic set, the translation error grows from 1.81.8 to 887887 mm, and the reconstructed deformation shrinks to 28%28\% of its true magnitude (97%97\% with the dedicated pathway). In addition, the failure is not a matter of numerical scale. Normalizing the rigid signal to unit variance before the shared compression barely helps (→49.652.8\!\rightarrow\!49.6 mm world error), whereas the dedicated linear pathway reaches 8.38.3 mm. The rigid and the deformation signals compete for the capacity of the shared latent, and the dedicated pathway removes this competition.

F.3 Spatial VAE pretraining

This section explains why the spatial VAE needs to be pretrained first rather than trained directly together with the ST-VAE. We compare two training schemes at a matched budget. The first pretrains the spatial VAE and then trains the ST-VAE on top of it with an additional latent-anchor loss (Sec. 3.3), which ties the per-frame latents reconstructed by the ST-VAE to those of the pretrained spatial VAE. The second trains both stages jointly from scratch, with a randomly initialized spatial VAE.

We find that joint training works poorly. At the standard learning rate, training diverges within a few thousand steps. At a reduced learning rate, it converges to a much worse model: the geometric reconstruction error is about 5×5\times that of the pretrained scheme, the deformation is much weaker than the ground truth, and volume is lost. The likely reason is that the two stages chase each other. The latent that the ST-VAE learns to reproduce keeps moving while the spatial VAE is still changing, so the temporal model has no fixed target. Pretraining fixes the target first. Once pretrained, the spatial VAE can either be kept frozen during ST-VAE training or fine-tuned with a smaller learning rate, and the two options give similar results. We keep it frozen for ST-VAE Small and fine-tune it for ST-VAE Base.

F.4 The spatial decoder GNN

We use a GNN component in the spatial VAE decoder because the field decoder places every vertex independently, so nothing ties neighboring vertices together, and the GNN over the tetrahedral mesh adds this coupling. We compare three placements of the GNN: in the decoder, as in our model; removed; and moved to the encoder instead. Without the GNN, reconstruction degrades and many mesh edges end up stretched far from their rest length. With the GNN in the encoder, the result is worse on every metric, because smoothing the mesh before encoding removes detail before it reaches the latent, whereas smoothing after decoding only regularizes the output.

Appendix G Inference Runtime

This section reports the inference speed of PhysLDM and how it depends on the mesh resolution. We measure batch-1 inference on a single H200 for 6464-frame trajectories on five held-out scenes with 980980 to 9,8519{,}851 vertices, the last three beyond the 5,0005{,}000-vertex training cap. One inference pass consists of three steps: the spatial VAE encodes frame 00, the latent model predicts the latent trajectory (one forward pass for the regression model, 5050 or 2020 Euler steps for the LDM), and the ST-VAE decodes all 6464 frames. Timings are medians over repeated runs with the GPU synchronized and no I/O in the timed region, in bf16 and in fp32. Table 10 lists the decoding time, the resulting frame rates, and the peak GPU memory.

Two observations follow. First, the cost of the latent model is independent of the mesh resolution, because it always works on the same 4,1044{,}104 latent tokens, so its latency is the same at every NN (bf16: 9.89.8 ms for the regression model, 460460 ms for the LDM at 2020 steps, and 1,1501{,}150 ms at 5050). The decoder is the only stage whose cost grows with NN, and in bf16 it is nearly flat, from 318318 ms at 980980 vertices to 384384 ms at 9,8519{,}851, with no loss of accuracy. As a result, the LDM runs at about 4040 to 8080 frames per second in bf16 and the regression model at up to 195195, even on meshes twice the training cap. Second, the whole pass needs only about 55 GiB of GPU memory across the range.

Appendix H Additional Qualitative Results

This section extends the qualitative figures of the main text with more scenes, lists the parameters of every scene shown, and presents the extreme case of Appendix I.

H.1 More reconstruction and prediction results

Figs. 9, 10, and 11 extend Figs. 3 and 4 with further scenes, rendered and laid out in the same way. Figs. 9 and 10 show ST-VAE reconstruction on four more scenes against every ST-VAE baseline of Table 7. Fig. 11 shows our prediction on four more scenes against the prediction baselines of Table 2. The observations of the main text hold on these scenes as well. The results of the standard baseline, its variants, and adaptive compression look reasonable in these static frames, but their DCC values (Table 7) show that they have the staircase artifact. The direct world-coordinate baseline produces noisy geometric detail. The regression model produces wrong physics and jitter, and the MGN-style AR baseline drifts over time. Tables 11 and 12 list the source dataset, node count, and simulation parameters of every scene in these figures and in the main-text figures.

The bottom-left block of Fig. 1 shows one-shot prediction on a larger set of objects in one scene. Twenty-six objects from GSO, Toys4K, and the held-out Objaverse scenes, with 1,5171{,}517 to 9,8219{,}821 nodes, are thrown onto a round stage with initial speeds between 0.570.57 and 1.871.87 m/s and Young’s moduli between 3×1043\times 10^{4} and 3×1063\times 10^{6} Pa, so that soft plush toys, a rubber boot, and a bunch of grapes share the scene with a helmet, a drill, and a cardboard box. The inset shows the initial state: every object in its undeformed rest shape, placed above the position where it will land, seen from the same camera as the main view. The main view shows the predicted state near the end of the sequence, when almost all objects have landed, rendered with the original textures of the assets. Each object is predicted independently as a 6464-frame trajectory from its initial state, and the soft objects deform visibly on landing while the stiff ones keep their shape.

Appendix I Extreme Cases Analysis

This section analyzes extreme cases. The accuracy of the LDM is fundamentally bounded by the reconstruction performance of the ST-VAE, meaning that the most challenging cases for the ST-VAE set the limits of the entire pipeline. Across the held-out scenes, the largest reconstruction errors mostly occur on geometries with many long, thin features.

Fig. 12 illustrates a representative extreme case, a soft birdcage comprising 9,0219{,}021 nodes, which is 1.81.8 times the 5,0005{,}000-vertex training cap and contains dozens of thin bars only a few tetrahedra thick. Its mean reconstruction error over the trajectory is 9.99.9 mm, about twice the held-out mean for meshes above the training cap (Table 1). This error is localized to the thin bars, which exhibit distorted and tangled reconstructions. Nevertheless, the overall shape of the collapsed cage, its pose, and its motion over the trajectory are all recovered.

Furthermore, node count alone is not the primary performance bottleneck. For instance, the teaser mug shown in Fig. 1 represents a compact solid with 11,62111{,}621 nodes (2.32.3 times the training cap) yet achieves a lower reconstruction error of 5.35.3 mm. What distinguishes the birdcage is the density of thin features that deform independently of each other. The folding of every bar is a high-frequency deformation, and the fixed-size latent has to carry it for dozens of bars at once. The latent has enough capacity for the global shape, but not for the fine detail of every bar.

Appendix J Multi-Body Extension

This section describes the multi-body extension of our method and presents its qualitative results. Our approach generalizes effectively to multi-object scenes. The factorization defined in Eq. (1) is applied at the scene level: a single global rigid transform (𝐑t,𝐜t)(\mathbf{R}_{t},\mathbf{c}_{t}) is fitted across the vertices of all bodies, while the relative motion among bodies is captured by the canonical deformation field 𝐝t\mathbf{d}_{t}. Because the spatial VAE encodes all vertices within a scene through a shared set of KK query tokens, multi-body scenes are encoded, compressed, and predicted in the same manner as single-body objects, requiring no architectural modifications to the ST-VAE or the LDM.

We train both the ST-VAE and the LDM on scenes containing up to three bodies (n≤3n\leq 3), where randomly selected objects are thrown toward each other to collide in mid-air before hitting the ground. Each body is assigned an independent random Young’s modulus and initial velocity.

Fig. 13 illustrates the ST-VAE reconstruction on four multi-body scenes across four representative frames: immediately before and after the mid-air collision, the first frame following ground impact, and the final settled state. All bodies within each scene, including their collisions and ground contacts, are successfully reconstructed through the single global transform. Fig. 14 demonstrates one-shot prediction on four multi-body scenes conditioned on the initial state, with predictions rendered using the original textured assets. The entire scene, encompassing each individual body along with its collision dynamics and landing behavior, is predicted end-to-end in a single diffusion pass.

Appendix K Differentiable Applications: Setup and Results

This section gives the setup and the full results of the two differentiable tasks of Sec. 4.2. Both tasks run on the same scene and use the same model. The first, material estimation, needs a first-order gradient. The second, designing the throw, needs a second-order gradient. Table 13 summarizes how our model and the two differentiable simulators, DiffIPC (Huang et al., 2024b) and Newton/Warp, behave on them.

K.1 Material estimation

The first task is to recover the Young’s modulus E⋆E^{\star} of a body from a single observed trajectory. Because EE enters our model through the scalar material channel, the mismatch between the predicted rollout and the observation is end-to-end differentiable with respect to log⁡E\log E. Starting from initial guesses up to 1.1 dex away from seven ground-truth moduli E⋆∈[3⋅104,3⋅106]E^{\star}\in[3{\cdot}10^{4},3{\cdot}10^{6}], our model successfully recovers all seven within 0.060.06 dex in just 40 Adam steps (∼\sim40 seconds). Figure 15 compares the observed, initial, and recovered trajectories and shows the estimation error across all seven moduli.

Existing differentiable simulators already have difficulty with this first-order task. DiffIPC does not converge under default settings and only runs stably after manual tuning of the solver parameters, and then needs about 26 minutes. Newton/Warp, meanwhile, fails on this task: it consumes massive memory (49 GB tape for 131k substeps) before its gradients explode through the complex dynamics simulation, resulting in random gradient signs and total optimization failure.

K.2 Beyond material estimation: designing the throw

Building on the first task, we ask a further question: which throw makes the stiffness easiest to estimate? A throw is informative when a small change in EE produces a large change in the resulting trajectory.

Task Setup.

Crucially, how large this trajectory change is depends on the stiffness of the body itself. Therefore, the trajectory sensitivity must be evaluated at a specific value of EE, which we set to E⋆E^{\star} (6⋅1046{\cdot}10^{4} Pa). The design is thus local: it finds the most informative throw for a body of roughly this stiffness, assuming a rough estimate of the stiffness is already available. To ensure robustness against launch errors, we maximize the sensitivity of the predicted rigid motion to log10⁡E\log_{10}E, averaged over eight small perturbations of the release velocity v0v_{0}. Because the objective itself is a derivative, maximizing it via gradient ascent fundamentally requires a second-order gradient.

Optimization Results.

Our model supports higher-order derivatives and provides this second-order gradient directly via reverse-mode automatic differentiation. In just 30 Adam steps (7 minutes), our model successfully optimizes the throw. Replaying this designed throw in the ground-truth solver confirms its effectiveness: the sensitivity of the rigid motion to EE increases by 13×13\times, and per-vertex sensitivity by 1.85×1.85\times. This highly informative trajectory significantly widens the basin of attraction, enabling successful EE recovery even from a distant initial guess (E0=106E_{0}=10^{6}) where the original throw stalls. Figure 16 visualizes the ground-truth trajectories of the initial and the optimized throw, the sensitivity gain, and the subsequent material-estimation runs from this distant initial guess.

Comparison with Differentiable Simulators.

If the first-order task is already this challenging for existing solvers, this second-order throw design becomes infeasible for them. DiffIPC is inherently limited to first-order analytic adjoints; forcing it to approximate the necessary second-order gradient requires nested finite differences (6464 forward solves per step). As a result, a single gradient step takes 2.4 hours, about 635×635\times slower than our model. The whole design would therefore take about three days, which is not acceptable in practice. For Newton/Warp, which already fails to produce a usable first-order gradient, such higher-order applications are insurmountable. In contrast, PhysLDM effortlessly scales to these advanced demands, acting as a fast, stable surrogate that natively supports higher-order derivatives. Table 13 summarizes the comparison on both tasks.

Appendix L Comparison with Concurrent Work

This section compares PhysLDM with the concurrent one-shot model of Chen et al. (2026). That model is a diffusion transformer with factorized spatiotemporal attention that denoises the full TT-frame trajectory directly on vertex×\timesframe tokens, without any latent, and it was trained on low-resolution surface meshes (about 356356 vertices per scene, 3535 templates). Because its cost grows with the number of vertices times the number of frames, it cannot be trained at the resolution of our dataset, so the two models cannot be compared directly on our full data. We therefore compare them in two steps. First, we measure the vertex count up to which the raw-coordinate formulation fits in memory at all. Second, we choose a resolution where it does fit, train both models on the same data there, and compare their training cost and generation quality.

L.1 Memory and resolution limits

Table 14 reports peak training memory and GPU time per sample at batch 11 (T=64T{=}64, bf16, flash attention, one 140140 GiB H200) for the published backbone of the concurrent work (DiT-L, 340340M parameters) and for its DiT-B variant (130130M, with the same width and depth as our LDM), for vertex counts from 500500 to 5,0005{,}000. The published backbone runs out of memory above 1,0001{,}000 vertices and the DiT-B variant above 2,7502{,}750. Neither fits the median scene of our dataset (∼3,400{\sim}3{,}400 vertices) even at batch 11, and the 5,0005{,}000-vertex cap is further out of reach. Our LDM works on the latent and trains at ∼4.4{\sim}4.4 GiB and ∼27{\sim}27 ms per trajectory at any vertex count.

L.2 Training setting and cost

At a resolution where the concurrent model does fit in memory, we train both models from scratch under the same conditions. We train the concurrent model’s DiT-B variant with their training procedure and our full three-stage pipeline on the same training scenes with at most 1,0001{,}000 vertices. The comparison is budget-matched: both models are trained on the same scenes on the same GPUs, the concurrent DiT-B has the same width and depth as our LDM, and each deploys its validation-selected checkpoint. Table 15 gives the training time of both. Our full three-stage pipeline trains in less time than the single-stage concurrent model, and most of our time goes to the ST-VAE rather than the LDM.

L.3 Prediction results comparison

Fig. 17 compares the predictions of the two models on four held-out scenes at this resolution, shown at the last frame of the trajectory. Both models place the object roughly where the ground truth places it. The difference is in the geometric detail. The concurrent model produces surfaces that are visibly noisy: the block bends and its faces ripple, the spoon and the shaft of the screwdriver are corrugated, and the bottle is lumpy. The zoom-in views show this noise on every surface. Our model keeps the shape of every object and its surfaces stay smooth.

The reason lies in where each model generates geometry. Our ST-VAE is pretrained to reconstruct shapes, so the decoder maps any latent it receives to a clean shape on the learned manifold. A small error in the latent predicted by the LDM therefore becomes a small, coherent change of the shape, and the geometric detail is preserved. The concurrent model predicts every vertex coordinate directly, so there is nothing between its prediction and the geometry. A small error in any coordinate appears on the surface as is, and the many small errors of a diffusion model add up to noisy geometric detail.

This problem is not visible in the concurrent work’s own demonstrations because meshes in their training data are simple and coarse, with at most a few hundred vertices, and the whole dataset is built from only a few dozen mesh templates. A model can learn these few simple shapes accurately with much less difficulty. On our data, with thousands of distinct objects at native resolution, learning the geometry itself becomes much harder.

L.4 Inference cost comparison

Our model is also much faster at inference. The concurrent model denoises N×64N\times 64 vertex tokens, so its latency grows with the mesh, whereas our LDM denoises the fixed 4,1044{,}104 latent tokens. On a scene of about 1,0001{,}000 vertices, our model predicts a 6464-frame trajectory in about 1.51.5 s at 5050 sampling steps and 0.80.8 s at 2020, while the concurrent model needs about 12.912.9 s and 5.15.1 s, so ours is roughly 9×9\times and 6×6\times faster.

Appendix M Training Across Energy Models and on Real Captured Trajectories

PhysLDM is trained with kinematic supervision only (Sec. 3.3). No energy model or material law enters the data format, the losses, or the architecture. This design gives PhysLDM three practical advantages, which we test in this section.

  1. 1.

    Diverse energy models. Because the constitutive model never enters training, the same pipeline can learn from simulations with any energy model.

  2. 2.

    Data without an explicit energy model. For the same reason, PhysLDM can learn from trajectories with only an implicit energy model, such as trajectories captured in the real world.

  3. 3.

    Seamless support for other data formats, such as surface meshes and point clouds. Our training data are tetrahedral meshes, but PhysLDM does not depend on the tetrahedra themselves. The spatial VAE only takes vertex positions and a graph over the vertices. For a tetrahedral mesh, the graph is given by the tetrahedral edges. A surface mesh fits this structure naturally, with its triangle edges as the graph. For a point cloud, we can use a kk-nearest-neighbor graph or no edges at all. PhysLDM therefore runs on these formats without any change to the model or the training code. Because our input does not need to be a tetrahedral mesh, PhysLDM also supports object types beyond volumetric solids, such as cloth and rope, which are usually not represented with tetrahedra.

We test these advantages in two steps. First, we apply the pretrained PhysLDM, trained only on Stable Neo-Hookean simulations of Objaverse meshes, to new data without any adaptation. Second, we fine-tune it on the new data with the unchanged training code.

M.1 Data

Diverse energy models. We take 4040 held-out Objaverse scenes and simulate each scene twice with StiffGIPC from the same initial state. The first run uses the Stable Neo-Hookean energy of the training data (Smith et al., 2018). The second run uses an as-rigid-as-possible (ARAP) energy (Sorkine and Alexa, 2007) with the same shear stiffness and no volume term, so the objects are softer and more compressible. The two energies move the trajectories 2828 mm apart (median over scenes). We exclude the chaotic scenes of Appendix D, so this difference comes from the energy model and not from solver noise.

Real captured point clouds. We use 2222 real captured sequences from Jiang et al. (2025): 99 soft volumetric objects (plush toys and a package), 88 pieces of cloth, and 55 ropes, each lifted, pushed, or stretched by a human hand on a table. The data are 3D points tracked over time with three RGB-D cameras, with 616616 to 7,8267{,}826 points per object. There is no mesh and no explicit energy model, and the forces of the human hand are not observed. The setting of these scenes is also very different from that of our training data. In our simulations, every object is released in the air with an initial velocity and falls onto the ground. In the captured sequences, the object rests on a table and is manipulated by a human hand. The real data are therefore out of domain for PhysLDM. We store the tracked points as the vertices and a kk-nearest-neighbor graph (k=8k=8) as the topology, in the same file format as our simulated data. PhysLDM is thus seamlessly compatible with these data, without any change to our code.

Evaluation. We use the metrics of Table 2 (Appendix B.4): the volume violation rate, the deformation-to-rigid kinetic energy ratio, and the world-coordinate error, each reported as the median over scenes. The first two need tetrahedra and are not defined on the point clouds.

M.2 Zero-shot results

Table 16 applies the pretrained PhysLDM to the new data without any adaptation.

The ST-VAE generalizes zero-shot across energy models and to real point clouds. On the simulated scenes, the reconstruction error is 4.54.5 mm with Stable Neo-Hookean and 4.64.6 mm with ARAP. On the real point clouds it is 6.06.0 mm. This is the most demanding test: the scenes show manipulation by a human hand instead of objects thrown onto the ground, the data are real captures instead of simulations, the input is a point cloud instead of a tetrahedral mesh, and cloth and rope never appear in training. Even on this out-of-domain data, the ST-VAE reconstructs the motion accurately without any adaptation. Although the ST-VAE was trained only on Stable Neo-Hookean simulations, it represents motion under an unseen energy model (ARAP) and real motion without an explicit energy model almost as accurately (Fig. 18). This shows that its latent space is not tied to the energy model of the training data.

The LDM prediction depends on the training data. On the simulated scenes with Stable Neo-Hookean, the prediction error is 23.923.9 mm, in line with Table 2. With ARAP, the error grows to 37.537.5 mm and the kinetic energy ratio drops to 0.790.79: the LDM predicts the deformation of the material it was trained on, while the ARAP objects deform more. On the real sequences, the zero-shot prediction fails (875875 mm) because of the domain gap, not the energy model. The LDM has only learned objects thrown onto the ground, while the real object stays on the table until the human hand moves it.

M.3 Fine-tuning with the unchanged pipeline

To adapt PhysLDM to new data, we only replace the training data with the new trajectories and fine-tune the LDM from the pretrained weights with the same trainer. The ST-VAE stays frozen. The same procedure applies to both energy models and to the real point clouds. Table 17 reports the results on the fine-tuning subsets, so the values before fine-tuning differ slightly from Table 16. For both explicit energy models, the prediction error drops by about two thirds, to 7.67.6 mm and 8.88.8 mm. For ARAP, the kinetic energy ratio moves from 0.800.80 to 0.920.92, so the LDM learns the softer material from the trajectories alone. On the real point clouds, the error drops from 921921 to 6.26.2 mm: the LDM learns from the tracked points that a resting object stays on the table and how the points move (Fig. 18).

In summary, the same PhysLDM, with the same code and losses, handles simulations with different energy models, real captured trajectories without an explicit energy model, and other data formats such as point clouds. Its ST-VAE transfers to all of them zero-shot, and its LDM adapts to them by fine-tuning. Visual results of PhysLDM on the real captured data are shown in Fig. 18.
